11535-views-a-foot-or-europe-seen-with-k:
J. Bayard Taylor's Views A-Foot was entered in 1846, with a preface by N. P. Willis. Willis praises a printer's apprentice turned traveller and author, whose talent he had spotted early. The book tells of Europe seen with knapsack and staff.

Part one moves from the voyage to a day in Ireland. Ben Lomond and the Highland lakes follow. Then the tour crosses the Continent, with frescoed halls at Munich recalling Charlemagne, Barbarossa, and Rudolph of Hapsburg. The book is a young American's walking tour, written with energy and a poet's eye.
15300-mike-flannery-on-duty-and-off:
Ellis Parker Butler's 1909 humor book follows Mike Flannery, an express office man at Westcote, on duty and off. Three stories, Just Like a Cat, The Three Hundred, and Fleas Will Be Fleas, make the set, with pictures by Gustavus Widney. A frontispiece jokes over the name Phoenix.

Flannery watches a land company rip the top off Seiler's Hill and dump it into a swampy meadow, soon to burst into streets and houses. Cats, helpers, and office talk supply the comedy. Readers who like Irish-American humor will find Mike warm, funny, and full of small-town bustle.
15971-polly-of-the-hospital-staff:
A children's hospital story by Emma C. Dowd, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1912, printed at the Riverside Press, Cambridge. Dowd dedicates the book to the Mother of Polly. Polly, a girl on the hospital staff, brings cheer to wards and nurses alike. Dowd writes with warmth for sick children and their helpers.

The cherry-pudding story and the election of Polly open the book, with Popover, David, and Lone Star's assistance. Elsie's birthday, the little sad lady, and a warning from Aunt Jane follow, with a night of song and the ward's anniversary. Polly plays Eva to close. The book delights as a hospital tale: a girl who heals by kindness, in a place of pain.
16197-one-third-off:
Irvin S. Cobb's 1921 Doran volume, illustrated by Tony Sarg, gathers humorous pieces with a telling frontispiece: the author weighing himself and crediting the scales with a profound shock. He dedicates the book to Harry M. Stevens, who in times gone by helped him put that one third on. Contents range from a plea for Old Cap Collier and the abandoned farmers to the life of the party, eating in two or three languages, and Europe revised.

Roughing it de luxe, Cobb's anatomy, and the thunders of silence show his range, from dieting and travel to small-town life and war talk. Cobb, famed for Old Judge Priest, writes warm, drawling American humor. Readers who like newspaper wit at its most companionable will enjoy this cheerful miscellany.
22879-paul-patoff:
F. Marion Crawford places Paul Patoff in the East in his 1887 novel. Even the horses feel the weather in the excerpt. Haroun al Raschid, a gray, shakes raindrops restlessly from his mane, longing, it seems, for hot sand and desert sun. The wind, another rider notes, is the wind of home.

Crawford knew Constantinople and Rome well, and he builds the tale on diplomatic and social ground between East and West. Paul Patoff, a Russian diplomat's son, moves through intrigue where manners and danger intertwine. Crawford's novels were international bestsellers, prized for polished scenes and cosmopolitan settings. This one offers melodrama with a traveler's eye, written by a man who had lived inside the world he describes.
6564-the-love-tiff:
Molière joins two pieces in this five-act comedy from 1656, first played at Béziers while the States General of Languedoc met there. The longer part borrows its plot from an Italian comedy, turning on a child swapped at birth, a trick that runs through many old plays and tales. The shorter, finer part is Molière's own, and it is the part the French stage still plays.

Lovers quarrel, servants scheme, and mistaken kinship keeps the plot in a spin until the truth unties it. The verse moves fast, and the jokes land through talk rather than through stage tricks. For readers new to Molière, The Love-Tiff shows both his debts to older comedy and his own fresh voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baroness-von-:
Baroness von Droste-Hülshoff was a poet, born at Schloss Hülshoff near Münster in 1797, who died in 1848. After her father's death in 1826, she lived mostly at Rüschhaus near Münster, with long visits to Meersburg on Lake Constance. Born prematurely, she carried a powerful mind in a delicate, sickly frame all her life. Her gifts joined inexhaustible imagination with keen observation and a quaint, facile poetic language.

Her uncles August and Werner von Haxthausen drew her into the romantic movement, and Sprickmann first trained her in verse. Schlüter, her longtime mentor, with Junkmann, first brought her poems before the public in 1838, though unhappily chosen. Later editions by Schücking, Kreiten, and Arens, plus her edited letters, secured her standing. Her Geistliches Jahr remained unfinished at her death, its concluding part left incomplete.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-freiherr-von-:
Josef von Eichendorff, called the last champion of romanticism, was a German poet and storyteller of the early nineteenth century. Born in 1788 at the family castle of Lubowitz in Upper Silesia, he studied at Halle and Heidelberg. There he fell in with the Romantic school and its leaders Görres, Arnim, and Brentano. His first poems appeared while he was still a student.

Eichendorff left books and law in 1813 to join the Lützow volunteers against Napoleon, and he marched again in 1815, entering Paris with the victors. After 1816 he served Prussia as a civil servant, first at Danzig and later in Berlin's ministry of worship. His best-loved work remains the novella about a good-for-nothing wanderer, Aus dem Leben eines Taugenichts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-dering:
George Dering Wolff, an editor born in West Virginia in 1822, carried German Reformed learning into Catholic journalism. Son of a Reformed divine, he graduated from Marshall College, studied law, and, though admitted to the bar, took a four-year theology course and became a Reformed minister. He followed Nevin's Mercersburg school, which treated Christ's Church as a living organism and sought to restore truths the Reformation had dropped.

Seeing his tenets' inconsistency at last, Wolff joined the Catholic Church in 1871. He edited Baltimore's Catholic Mirror, then Philadelphia's Catholic Standard until his death as editor-in-chief. In 1876 he helped Corcoran and O'Connor found the American Catholic Quarterly Review. His pieces ran largely to apologetic theology. His wife and his brother also became Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-philip:
George Philipp Ludolf von Beckedorff, a Prussian official born at Hanover in 1778, rose high, converted, and was cast out. After theology at Jena and a medical degree at Göttingen in 1799, he tutored Anhalt-Bernburg's crown prince from 1810, then entered Prussia's High Privy Council and Ministry of Public Worship. As schools supervisor with Nicolovius he lifted popular education and issued a nine-volume Year Book of the Prussian Schools.

Study of the sects convinced Beckedorff that Rome was the true apostolic Church, and a beloved child's death decided him. After days with Bishop Sailer he abjured and communicated in June 1827, and dismissal followed at once. Retired to Grünhof, he built a church and school for scattered Catholics and poor children. Under Frederick William he regained honor, nobility, and the state agricultural department's presidency. His Catholic Truth, Words of Peace, ran three editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-llandaff:
Llandaff is an ancient Welsh diocese whose roots lie in the sixth-century monastic movement led by Dubricius. His pupil Teilo became abbot of the daughter house at Llandaff, which grew into the chief monastery after Dubricius withdrew to Bardsey.

Early abbots held episcopal rank, and Teilo and Dubricius are even called archbishops, though the title then meant rule over monasteries, not a province. Welsh bishops long stood apart from Rome's missionaries, and only in 768 took the Roman Easter reckoning. After the Norman Conquest, Canterbury claimed oversight, and Llandaff became its suffragan under Bishop Urban.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mohileff:
Mohileff was the Latin Catholic archdiocese and church province for Catholics under Russian rule. This entry follows its tangled birth and troubled history. Before Poland's partition, only scattered mission stations served Russia's few Catholics. Jesuits laboured in Moscow from 1648 and built its first Catholic church in 1691.

After the partitions brought hundreds of thousands of Catholics under the tsars, Empress Catherine set up the Diocese of White Russia at Mohileff in 1772. She acted without consulting the pope, then raised it to an archdiocese a decade later. Rome eventually recognised it. Later rulers squeezed it hard, suppressing sees and leaving archdioceses vacant for years. Only the 1905 toleration edicts eased the pressure, and local officials soon whittled that easing away.
doe-osti-3015048-measuring-the-energy-co: Neural nets got energy-metered, and this DOE text measures consumption and efficiency. The pages detail the empirical findings. The AI folks get their recommendations. The networks were deep neural. The recommendations were AI. The analysis was empirical. The recommendations were design.
doe-osti-3015810-gateway-cities-unplugge: Gateway cities got (em)powered, and this DOE final unplugs affordable housing. The pages detail the technical findings. The planners get their closeout. The housing was affordable. The closeout was planner. The cities were gateway. The report was technical. The housing was DOE's.

The energy folks get their closeout. The nation was Indian. The closeout was energy. The efficiency were project. The final were technical.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MeekJeff_Meek_J: A letter dated April 28, 1979 concerns the manuscript of John Joerg, and it is filed under the name Jeff Meek. Letters about manuscripts in these files usually pass between researchers, editors, and would-be publishers of assassination work. The file gives the date and the manuscript's author. It does not name the letter's writer or say what stage the manuscript had reached, so its contents cannot be described further.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Inside Chiquita's Colombia operation, staff on the ground were uneasy about money the company paid to armed groups. Michael Evans edited this briefing book, posted in May 2017, from the company's own papers. Top executives, the records show, grew comfortable with the payments even as questions rose.

Staff in Colombia asked whether Chiquita had gone past paying extortion. They feared the company was directly funding leftist guerrillas and right-wing paramilitary groups alike. That split between worried local staff and calm headquarters is the heart of the record, and it shows how a payment scheme looks from inside the firm that ran it.
michael-strogoff:
Jules Verne published Michael Strogoff in 1876, as part of his Extraordinary Voyages series. The novel opens at a brilliant fete in the New Palace at St. Petersburg. Word arrives that the telegraph wire is cut beyond Tomsk. A Tatar rebellion led by the Khan Feofar is rising in Siberia.

The Czar chooses his courier Michael Strogoff for a desperate mission. Strogoff must cross rebellious Siberia to reach besieged Irkutsk. There he must warn the Czar's brother about a traitor. The publisher's note calls it one of Verne's best books, and its ride across Russia made it famous.
mike-flannery-on-duty-and-off:
Ellis Parker Butler published this story collection with Doubleday, Page and Company in 1909. Its hero is Mike Flannery, the express agent at Westcote. The book holds three long tales: Just Like a Cat, The Three Hundred, and Fleas Will Be Fleas. Gustavus C. Widney supplied the illustrations.

In the opening story, Flannery watches workmen tear the top off Seiler's Hill behind his office. Their wagons dump clay into a swamp that will soon become streets and houses. Flannery hopes the growth will finally earn him real help. Butler tells his tales in Flannery's Irish-American voice, mixing small-town business with broad comedy.
nasa-tm-19710020807-flight-investigation:
Nick E. Samanich and Roger Chamberlin of the Lewis Research Center wrote this flight study, NASA TM X-2295, on a plug nozzle mounted beneath a wing. Several nozzle configurations were installed on an underwing nacelle of an F-106B aircraft. A J85 turbojet engine supplied the exhaust flow for the tests.

The team compared installed performance with isolated cold-flow results from a scale model in a Lewis wind tunnel. They varied plug truncation, shroud extension, secondary cooling flow, and nozzle pressure ratio, and also changed the nacelle shape ahead of the nozzle. The summary reports that installation had little effect near the top of the subsonic range. It hurt at lower speeds and just above Mach one. Installed performance actually peaked higher than the isolated data, thanks to pressure effects from the wing and nacelle flow fields.
one-third-off:
Irvin Shrewsbury Cobb wrote this book of wit and humor. George Doran published his works in New York. The frontispiece shows Cobb weighing himself with shock. Its caption jokes that he credited himself a profound shock. The title promises a plea from a man reducing.

Cobb lists earlier books of fiction, humor, and miscellany. Titles include Old Judge Priest and Cobb's Anatomy. Eating in several languages is one comic theme here. The abandoned farmers and the life of the party follow. Cobb was a famed American humorist and journalist. His self-mockery made dieting a source of laughter.
polly-of-the-hospital-staff:
Emma C. Dowd published Polly of the Hospital Staff in Boston with Houghton Mifflin in 1912, dedicating it to the mother of Polly. Her heroine is a small, lame girl whose cherry-pudding story opens the book and whose election by the children's ward follows: the patients themselves choose Polly as their sunbeam. Contents move through birthdays, a little sad lady, a night of song, and Polly playing Eva in a ward performance.

Trouble comes with a kidnapping and a bid for Polly, since a lovable child in a hospital is a child several households want. The illustrations list ends with a document that makes her legally a daughter, and the contents end with a wedding, the staff's own. Dowd wrote sunshine literature with a purpose: to show cheerfulness as a form of care. Polly's success made her the first of a line of glad girls in American children's books.
song-of-roland-scott-moncrieff:
The Song of Roland, France's oldest great epic, was composed around 1140 and survives in the Oxford manuscript. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation renders its ringing verse. The poem sings of Charlemagne's Spanish campaign of 778 and the ambush at Roncesvalles.

Roland, the emperor's nephew, leads the rear guard through the Pyrenees pass. Betrayed by Ganelon, he faces a vast Saracen host and refuses, from pride, to blow his horn for help until too late. His death, sword Durendal in hand, is the poem's summit. Charlemagne's vengeance and Ganelon's trial close the song. It founded the whole line of French chansons de geste.
the-love-tiff:
The Love-Tiff is an English version of Molière's Le Dépit amoureux, a comedy in five acts first represented at Béziers toward the end of 1656. An introductory notice explains that the play joins two pieces. The longer part modestly imitates a coarse Italian comedy, L'Interesse by Nicolo Secchi, and turns on a girl substituted for a boy, a device Shakespeare also used.

The notice praises the parts that are Molière's alone, including the quarrel between Éraste and Lucile that gives the play its title, and their reconciliation. It also puzzles over earlier translators who renamed the servant Gros-René, one calling him punch-gutted Ben and another Hugh. Plot, the notice admits, is over-complicated and the ending unnatural, yet the characters move through errors with no visible way out.
views-a-foot-or-europe-seen-with-knapsac:
J. Bayard Taylor wrote Views A-Foot, or Europe Seen with Knapsack and Staff, a young man's walk across Europe in two parts. Copyright was entered in 1846 by Wiley and Putnam at New York. N. P. Willis, who wrote the preface, says the book needs little introduction, since it tells its own story well. His interest, he admits, is that of an early fan of Taylor's talent.

Willis recalls that Taylor's poems, written while he was still a printer's apprentice, struck him hard, and that he praised them in the newspaper he then edited. Letters followed, and then friendship. The motto from The Winter's Tale urges the walker to jog on and keep a merry heart, since a merry heart goes all the day. Readers get the record of a poor, keen American seeing the old world on foot, with a famous editor's blessing at the door.
